title: How to stack 4 books so the top one is off the table
description:
Stack four books so the top one sits completely past the table's edge, no glue. A stack stays up while its middle is over whatever holds it, so build from the top down: with 24 cm books, the top one sticks out 12 cm (half), the top two together 6 more, three 4 more, and four 3 more past the table. 12 + 6 + 4 + 3 = 25 cm, a centimetre more than a whole book. The steps are halves of 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4..., the harmonic series, so the overhang never stops growing, just slows: 31 books reach two lengths, 227 reach three.

Numbers checked in code (exact fractions, a balance check for every sub-stack, and 200,000 random 4-book stacks, none of which beat 25/24). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block-stacking_problem

facts_checked: Maximum overhang of n identical blocks = sum of 1/(2i), i = 1..n (block lengths); 4 blocks = 25/24, the first n past one length (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block-stacking_problem)
24 cm books: steps 12, 6, 4, 3 cm, total 25 cm, 1 cm past the edge; 3 books reach only 22 cm (verify.py)
Balance: the centre of the top k books sits exactly over the edge of the support below, k = 1..4 (verify.py)
Blocks needed for 1, 2, 3 lengths: 4, 31, 227 (Wikipedia, OEIS A014537; verify.py)
200,000 random stable 4-book stacks: best 1.02 lengths, none beats 25/24 (verify.py)

beats.say: Stack 4 books so the top one is fully off the table.
No glue, no tape, no weight on the back. It's all about where each book's middle sits.
Here's the rule. A stack stays up as long as its middle is over whatever holds it. So build from the top down.
Your books are 24 centimetres long. Slide the top one out 12, half its length. Its middle now sits right on the edge below.
Now the top two move as one. Their shared middle is 6 in from the end, so they go out 6 more.
Three books: 4 more. And all four: 3 more, past the edge of the table.
12, then 6, then 4, then 3. Is that enough to clear a whole book?
Add it up: 25 centimetres. The top book hangs a full centimetre past the table. More books keep going, forever, each step smaller than the last.
So how many books do you need to stick out two whole lengths?
